notes.title: Orinduik: Navitas option and the Guyana licence (12 Nov 2026)

sections.heading: Where things stand
paragraphs: The Eco–Navitas framework was signed in early December 2025. Navitas paid US$2m for options over Orinduik and Block 1 CBK, the Orange Basin block off South Africa. The Orinduik option is exercisable within 12 months for US$2.5m and gives Navitas 80% and operatorship, carrying Eco's 20% up to US$11m net, excluding mobilisation.
The Block 1 CBK farm-down completed on 22 September 2026. Navitas took 37.5% and operatorship, paid US$4m in cash, and will carry Eco for up to US$7.5m net.

The Orinduik licence expired on 14 January 2026 at the end of its second renewal. Eco says the Petroleum Act keeps its rights to the Jethro-1 and Joe-1 discoveries (2019, heavy oil) while its appraisal programme is reviewed.

On 22 May 2026 the minister, Vickram Bharrat, said no extension was granted for Orinduik or Canje. Canje expired on 4 March 2026; Eco has an indirect interest in Canje through JHI Associates. Both blocks must apply for new licences under the new production sharing agreement (PSA).

Eco had guided a new PSA by September, in the third quarter. On 1 October the minister confirmed that none had been issued. Eco says talks are progressing well. Nothing newer was found as of 12 November 2026.

sections.heading: Why it is slow
sections.label: Analyst read
paragraphs: This section is an analyst read, not a reason given by the government. The government has given no stated reason for this delay.

Guyana has been deliberately tougher on terms after criticism of the Exxon Stabroek deal. The old Orinduik terms were a 1% royalty, a 75% cost-recovery cap, and no corporate income tax, with the state paying the company's tax from its profit oil. The new PSA has a 10% royalty, a 10% corporate tax and a 65% cost-recovery cap. Moving onto the new terms means a renegotiation, not a rollover, and makes the economics of appraising heavy oil harder.

Other factors also point the same way: a small energy ministry stretched by Exxon's new projects, the 2022 licensing round and the gas-to-shore project; caution after the 2025 election about signing anything that looks like a giveaway; and caution offshore given Venezuela's claim over the Essequibo region.

sections.heading: Any falling-out?
paragraphs: There is no sign of a falling-out. Neither side has publicly criticised the other, and Eco has described the talks as constructive and progressing well. The same treatment was applied to the Canje block, so Eco has not been singled out.
The only point of tension is Eco's view that it keeps its rights to the two discoveries, against the ministry's line that the licence "has come to an end". Neither side has escalated it.

sections.heading: Likely path
sections.label: Analyst judgement
paragraphs: The figures below are the author's judgement, not figures from any source.
About 50–60%: the December option deadline is extended, or the terms are amended, tied to the licence award. This is the most likely path.
About 25–30%: Guyana issues the new PSA before December and Navitas exercises close to the original terms.
About 15–20%: the option lapses, Eco keeps Orinduik and looks for another partner or a sole-risk path.
The reason is that Navitas is unlikely to pay US$2.5m and take on a carry of up to US$11m before it knows the new fiscal terms. Both sides still want the deal, as shown by the Block 1 CBK completion.
Things to watch: any Guyana statement on the Orinduik PSA, and Eco's December update around the option deadline.
